This unassuming little knife is an AKC, Italian-made lock back:

http://i.imgur.com/b0lqNnu.jpg

It's an auto of course, a more traditional design that the usual Italian classic, 1950s stabby patterns. (That's not the factory edge BTW):

http://i.imgur.com/DA26HpA.jpg

Quality is about the same as the other decent Italian autos. One the one hand, it's held together with peened pins that stand a little proud, and one of the horn scales is beginning to pull away. The safety quickly became loose and essentially useless as an actual safety device, and the firing button is very tall and easy to press when carried in the pocket. (When I do carry it, I place it in a little cloth pouch, and put that in my pocket, so that all my parts remain attached). The steel is a bit soft but not bad, and the slender blade profile allows it to cut well. It resharpens quickly on the bottom of a coffee cup. You can see how thick the handle is here:

http://i.imgur.com/uAStVRw.jpg

On the other hand, despite its flaws, it's a strangely endearing little knife.

It opens quickly and positively, and when open there is no discernible blade play, which frankly surprised me. The lock is positive and secure. It fits the hand and the pocket very well, and it has a certain charm that makes it feel like something more than the sum of its parts. I like it enough that I have a second one, in stag, tucked away in the safe.

http://i.imgur.com/V7EwSYb.jpg

These are not easy knives to find, although there were once several varieties available, mostly similar patterns with multiple blades in various combinations. There are a couple like this one available on gunbroker.com now, between $70 and $100. Search for both "speed hunter" and "speedhunter" to find them.

Manufacturer's site, including specs and a nice little video:

http://www.akc.it/speedhunter.html

Skipping classics here.

Reread: Heralds of Valdemar

Recommend: The Deed of Paksenarrion

Remember (for some absurd reason): Wizard's Bane (or rather, the Wiz Biz series. Not really fantasy, but meh.)

And yes, I cheated, These are all not really single books.

For pure fantasy I really liked the Wheel of Time books.

For something different try the Disc World books.

E. Forgot why. For WoT books it is a very large series with many different characters and a very developed world. For Disc World it's because they are funny as hell and insightful.
I agree with you, WoT is an amazing series. One of the few series in my opinion that can challenge the King of Fantasy crown from aSoIaF.

Hmmm. Tough one. I really enjoyed William's Memory, Sorrow, and Throne series, but I like WoT a lot more because, I think, it has a lot more scope to it. Overall, asking this question is like asking a mother which child is her favourite. She likes them all, but for different reasons.
The Book of Three by Lloyd Alexander. It not only is a perfect example of heroic fantasy, but it kicks off a fantastic series of books.
I had to forgotten about the Black Cauldron books. Good call.

The book that currently holds the title of the best book I ever read is In The Name of the Wind by Patrick Rothfuss. It is the first book of an trilogy. The second book is finished and available and the third book is about a year out I think. Always the book I recommend to anyone that asks. I also devour all of Jim Butchers books because they are fun to read.
Ignoring the classics, probably The First Law trilogy. That or American Gods. They were just such a huge change from what I was used to reading.

The Coldfire Trilogy by C. S. Friedman really stuck with me. The way she makes the characters eat their words is wonderful and so satisfying. Plus there are some really vivid, memorable scenes. Two come to mind, that are creepier than some horror stories I've read.
Dragonlance Chronicles, I love campy high-fantasy DnD novels.

The Malazan Book of the Fallen. It's hard to nail down just one reason why, so here's a few:

A vast, and yet incredibly detailed world with tons of interesting history. Erikson's and Esslemont's backgrounds as archaeologists (as well as Erikson's background as an anthropologist) make for a very plausible depiction of societies, especially the more primitive ones.

Warrens are a super interesting concept, as not just a source of magic but also as realms of their own.

Erikson constantly showing pretty much every trope out there the middle finger.

Deep character development, even of minor characters.

An almost fanatic devotion to the "show-don't-tell" style of writing. Erikson doesn't hold your hand and if he does any exposition it's generally done through natural conversation.

Hard-hitting philosophical musings on compassion, war, friendship and so much more.

A ton of amazingly badass characters. I won't even try to list any because there's just so damn many.

A mindblowing amount of foreshadowing. You don't even catch a fraction of it the first way through, and indeed for a first time reader I'd recommend just enjoying the ride. But on a reread you get all of these seemingly throwaway lines that turn out to be a direct reference to a future event. Sometimes an event that's waaaay in the future. I'm talking several books further in the series.

I could go on but this post would end up too long for anyone to read.

Like a few others, I have to go with The Wheel of Time. I been with the series from book One, rereading it at least each time the next one came out, and frequent have gotten others to start and read the series. So one level is the fact that I grew up with the characters, literally- I was the same age as the boys when they started. It was a well written series with important NPCs and multiple threads to follow. To choose a particular one in the series would be hard, but threadline would be easier. Mat would be first to the list, the lucky bastard. Perrin(especially after the Tinkers) comes in second.
